title: खस जातिको लोकसाहित्य र संस्कृतिका  बिच अन्तर्सम्बन्ध {Folklore and culture of Khas caste Interrelationships between}
nepali: खस आधुनिक मानवको पहिलो चरणमा विकसित ककेसियन, मङ्गोल, नेग्रो र आष्ट्रिक चार मूल जातिमध्ये ककेसियनका विभिन्न शाखाहरूमध्येको आदिम आर्य जातिकै एउटा शाखा कश अर्थात्अवैदिक आर्य जाति हो। आरम्भमा मध्य एसियाको युराल पर्वतमाला, ककेसस सेरोफेरोमा बस्ने ककेसियनहरू त्यहाँबाट बिस्तारै संसारभर फैलिएका देखिन्छन्। यीमध्य एउटा शाखा शक र कशमा विभाजित भएर इरान, मेसोपोटामिया आदि स्थानतर्फ फैलियो। तिनै आर्यबाट इरान नामकरण हुन पुग्यो। तीमध्ये एउटा शाखा शक इरानबाट मध्य भारतको गङ्गा नदीको मैदानमा आएर बस्यो र उसले त्यहाँ लौकिक परम्परामा रहेका वेदका ऋचाहरू निर्माण ग¥यो। अर्को शाखा कश मध्य भारतमा आएर वेद निर्माण गर्नुपूर्व नै फाटेर काश्मीर र काश्मीरसँगका भूभागसहितको बाल्हिक क्षेत्रमा आएर बस्यो। वेद निर्माण हुनुपूर्व नै फाटेर अर्को बाटो लागेकाले कश अर्थात्कालान्तरमा खस बनेको यस शाखाका वैदिक संस्कारहरू थिएनन् तर वेद निर्माण गर्नुपूर्व शाखा विभाजन नहुँदैका लौकिक परम्परामा रहेका यी दुवै थरीका साझा संस्कार र संस्कृति नै खस शाखाले पालन गर्दै रह्यो जसमध्ये कैयौँ वेदका अपरिष्कृत पूर्वरूप हुन्। ती संस्कारलाई खस जातिले लोकसाहित्यका आज प्रचलित मागल, धमारी, फाग, सगुन नाम दिइएका गीतका साथमा प्रयोगमा ल्यायो। यसरी खस जातिले जन्मदेखि मृत्युसम्मका शोडष संस्कारभन्दा पनि धेरै कर्ममा सयौँ मागल, फाग आदि गाएर कलात्मक ढङ्गले पूरा गर्न थाल्यो। यसैले खस जातिको लोकसाहित्य र संस्कार एवम्संस्कृतिको गहिरो सम्बन्ध छ ।
american_english: Among the four primary races developed in the initial stage of modern humans—Caucasian, Mongoloid, Negroid, and Australoid—the Khas is Kash, that is, a non-Vedic Aryan group, which is a branch of the primitive Aryans from among the various branches of Caucasians. Initially dwelling in the Ural mountain range and Caucasus surroundings of Central Asia, Caucasians appear to have gradually spread across the world from there. Divided into Shaka and Kash, one branch among these spread toward places such as Iran and Mesopotamia. From those very Aryans, Iran came to be named. Among them, one branch, the Shaka, came from Iran and settled in the plains of the Ganges River of central India, and there it composed the Vedic hymns that existed in folk tradition. Even before arriving in central India and creating the Vedas, the other branch, Kash, branched off and settled in the Bahlika region including Kashmir and territories adjoining Kashmir. Because it split off and took a different path before the creation of the Vedas, this Kash branch—which over time became the Khas—did not have Vedic rituals; however, the Khas branch continued to observe the shared rituals and culture of both these groups that existed in folk tradition before the branch division prior to the creation of the Vedas, many of which are unrefined prototypes of the Vedas. The Khas community brought those rituals into practice alongside the songs designated today in folklore as Magal, Dhamari, Phag, and Sagun. In this way, the Khas people began to artistically complete many more rites than the sixteen sacraments from birth to death by singing hundreds of Magal, Phag, and other songs. Therefore, there is a deep relationship between the folklore, rituals, and culture of the Khas people.

informal_english: Among the four main races that developed in the early stage of modern humans—Caucasian, Mongoloid, Negroid, and Australoid—the Khas is Kash, which is a non-Vedic Aryan group from the primitive Aryan branches of Caucasians. Initially living around Central Asia's Ural Mountains and the Caucasus area, Caucasians seem to have slowly spread out all over the world from there. Divided into Shaka and Kash, one branch of these headed off toward places like Iran and Mesopotamia. Iran actually got its name right from those Aryans. Among them, one branch, the Shaka, came from Iran and settled in the Ganges river plains of central India, where it composed the Vedic hymns that had been in folk tradition. Even before getting to central India and creating the Vedas, the other branch, Kash, broke off and settled in the Bahlika region along with Kashmir and neighbouring territories. Because it split off and took a different path before the Vedas were created, this Kash branch—which eventually became the Khas—didn't have Vedic rituals, but the Khas branch kept right on following the shared rituals and culture of both groups that existed in folk tradition before the division prior to the creation of the Vedas, many of which are unpolished earlier versions of the Vedas. The Khas folks put those rituals into practice alongside the songs known in folklore today as Magal, Dhamari, Phag, and Sagun. In this way, the Khas people began artistically performing way more rites than just the sixteen rituals from birth to death by singing hundreds of Magal, Phag, and other songs. That's why there is such a deep connection between the folklore, rituals, and culture of the Khas people.
